title: Good Works: Definition, Nature, and Evidence of Faith
speaker: Mr. Isaiah Couch

outline.title: The Definition of Good Works
subpoints: Good works are defined solely by God's commandments in His Word.
Works devised by men out of blind zeal or good intention are not good works.
Obedience to the revealed Word is superior to human tradition or ritual.

outline.title: The Nature of Good Works
subpoints: Good works are the fruit and evidence of a true and lively faith.
They are not the merit for salvation but the 'letter of credibility' of faith.
Believers manifest thankfulness and strengthen their assurance through obedience.

outline.title: The Purpose of Good Works
subpoints: Good works adorn the profession of the gospel and glorify God.
They serve as a visible light to the world, leading others to glorify the Father.
The ultimate end of good works is holiness and eternal life.

summary: In this Sunday School lesson, Mr. Isaiah Couch continues the series on the Westminster Confession of Faith, focusing on Chapter 16 regarding Good Works. Using the anchor passage of Ephesians 2:8-10, the teaching emphasizes that Christians are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that He prepared beforehand. The sermon employs the analogy of a sailing ship to illustrate that the Christian life is not meant to remain static in the harbor but to actively sail out in obedience to God's charted course.
transcript: Good morning and a happy Lord's Day, everyone. It is once again a joy to be able to speak during our Sunday school class. And before we begin, let's go ahead and open with prayer. Our Almighty God, we do thank you for this beautiful Lord's Day that you have commanded us to honor and set apart for our good and for your glory. And we ask that your spirit would open all of our hearts this morning as we open your word. May we see marvelous things contained within. Bless the teachers who are leading our children and bless our time here. And I pray that this frail and fragile vessel would be made nothing as we behold you. We pray this in your name. Amen. Well, this morning in our series, we continue through our confession of faith. And we will be looking at chapter 16 and good works. Thus far, we have covered chapters 9 through 15, which have discussed free will, effectual calling, justification, adoption, sanctification, saving faith, and repentance unto life. And as we begin this morning, I ask that you would please open your Bibles to Ephesians 2, verses 8 through 10. This will be our anchor passage throughout the entirety of our lesson this morning. Ephesians 2, verses 8 through 10. We read there, For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them. This morning as we look at this anchor passage for our lesson, we will examine the definition, the nature, the ability, the limitation, and the acceptance of good works. And while it is true that every analogy is imperfect, I want us to picture the Christian as a sailing ship. A ship that is designed to sail is just to do that. It is to sail. It is not designed to sit in the harbor tied to the pier. The same is true of the Christian. We are created in Christ Jesus for good works. A brother or sister who only talks about the things of God but never casts off and sets sail has mistaken the harbor for the ocean. Thomas Watson once said that works are faith's letter of credibility. In the same way that a sailing vessel would possess a letter of credibility from its sovereign, good works in the life of the Christian are their letter of credibility of a living and saving faith, graciously given to them by the sovereign Lord who rules over all. A ship that never leaves the harbor has denied the purpose for which it was created. And so while our goal this morning is simple, the application of these truths will show whether we are people who truly understand what it means to glorify God in thought, word, and deed. We must not sit in the harbor with our frail vessels loaded with the precious gems found in the word of God and never set sail on the ocean of life. But rather, we are to take those precious truths and set sail on this ocean, our vocation, our family, our friendships, our community, and our world. Always trusting that even when mighty tides about me sweep and perils lurk within the deep, angry clouds o'ershade the sky and the tempest rises high, Still I stand the tempest shock, for my anchor grips the rock. And so let us begin by looking at the definition of good works as contained in our confession of faith. Section 1, their definition. Before a ship can sail a true course, it must know which waters the king has charted for it. The definition of good works is not in zeal or sincerity or approval from men, but by the commandments of God revealed in his word alone. Since it is God who prepared the good works of Ephesians 2.10, it is God alone who defines them. And so our confession rightly says, Good works are only such as God has commanded in his holy word, and not such as, without the warrant thereof, are devised by men out of blind zeal or upon any pretense of good intention. The assembly observes here the clear line between the works God has prepared beforehand that men walk in compared to that which men invent. A ship that has no defined heading is ultimately blind. The same is true of man in his zeal or pretense of good intention apart from the word of God. Micah 6.6-8 declares this when it says, With what shall I come before the Lord and bow myself before the high God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, ten thousand rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the Lord require of you but to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God? The prophet Micah will not let Israel substitute the works that God has commanded and requires of men. The ship without a proper heading may appear like it knows the course, but it is not sailing the sovereign God's way. The apostle Paul, in Romans 12, 1-2, beseeches the brethren, saying, I beseech ye therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service. And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God. The king's vessel must not be conformed to this world. We are set apart for the good works that our God prepared beforehand. We may think of Nadab and Abihu in Leviticus 10, 1-2, when they offered strange fire before Yahweh, which he had not commanded of them. And so our reasonable service is to do only what Yahweh has commanded of us in his word, which alone is pleasing in his sight. Our Lord exposes false works in Matthew 15, 7-9 when he says, Hypocrites, well did Isaiah prophesy about you, saying, These people draw near to me with their mouth and honor me with their lips, but their heart is far from me, and in vain they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. The commandments of men cannot be defined as good works simply by calling them worship. When the good works that God prepared beforehand are replaced by tradition or blind zeal, the vessel may seek to fly the king's banner, but it bears the banner of the king falsely. Samuel's words speak of this to Saul in 1 Samuel 15 when he drives this truth even deeper so Samuel said has the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in obeying the voice of the Lord behold to obey is better than sacrifice and to heed than the fat of rams for rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry because you have rejected the word of the Lord, he also has rejected you from being king. Saul had, as our confession says, a pretense of good intention, but the Lord declared it for what it was, rebellion. Works that look like worship but have replaced the word of God is attempted mutiny against the king. Paul's grief over Israel in Romans 10, 1-3 shows this. When he says, brethren, My heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For they, being ignorant of God's righteousness and seeking to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted to the righteousness of God. And so Paul shows here that blind zeal and tradition are not the path that God has prepared beforehand. Seeking to establish our own righteousness is the opposite of Ephesians 2, 8-10. We are saved by grace, through faith, not by our own works. And so section 1 observes that the definition of good works is anchored here. We are his workmanship created in Christ Jesus for good works which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them. It is therefore God alone who defines and charts the course of what is pleasing to him Moving now to section two we going to examine their nature Here we see the nature and evidence of the true course and what it does in a people transformed by God's workmanship. Good works are not the merit for saving faith, but the fruit and evidence, or as Watson said, the letter of credibility of saving faith. And so our confession says, These good works done in obedience to God's commandments are the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith. And by them, believers manifest their thankfulness, strengthen their assurance, edify their brethren, adorn the profession of the gospel, stop the mouths of the adversaries, and glorify God, whose workmanship they are, created in Christ Jesus their unto, that having their fruit unto holiness, they may have the end, eternal life. This is a beautifully worded statement by the assembly. The good works that the believer walks in are the evidence, the letter of credibility of a true and lively faith, showing that we are the master shipbuilder's workmanship. Psalm 116 shows this evidence when the psalmist asks, What shall I render to the Lord for all his benefits towards me? I will take up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Notice that the psalmist does not ask what he shall render in order to obtain benefits from God. He asks what shall he render for the glorious benefits already received as he takes up the blessed cup of salvation. 1 John 2, 3-6 declares, Now by this we know that we know him if we keep his commandments. He who says, I know him and does not keep his commandments is a liar and the truth is not in him. But whoever keeps his word, truly the love of God is perfected in him. By this we know that we are in him. He who says he abides in him ought himself also to walk just as he walked. We do not keep God's commandments in order to become known by God. we keep his commandments because we are already known by him. Good works, that letter of credibility, shows that we are his in Christ Jesus. 2 Peter 1, 5-11 presses upon this same truth when it says, But also for this very reason, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge self-control, to self-control perseverance, to perseverance, godliness, to godliness, brotherly kindness, add to brotherly kindness, love. For if these things are yours and abound, you will be neither barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For he who lacks these things is short-sighted, even to blindness, and has forgotten that he was cleansed from his old sins. Therefore, brethren, be even more diligent to make your call and election sure. For if you do these things, you will never stumble. For so an entrance will be supplied to you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ. Peter does not tell us to add these things in order to be of the elect. He tells us that the elect make their calling and election sure if these things are yours and abound. You will be neither barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. Matthew 5, 14 through 16 shows how the nature of these good works adorn the gospel and glorify the Father. We read, you are the light of the world. A city that is set on a hill cannot be hidden, nor do they light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a lampstand, and it gives light to all who are in the house. Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven. The world sees the good works that God has prepared when we obediently walk in them. They themselves do not become authors of grace. Rather, they glorify the Father who is the author of grace. A ship that is darkened and says, we have fellowship with him. They lie and do not practice the truth. 1 John 1.6 Romans 6.20-23 names the glorious end which good works tend. For when you were a slave of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness. What fruit did you have then in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now having been set free from sin and having become slaves of God, you have your fruit to holiness and the end everlasting life. For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. And so eternal life remains the gracious and unmerited gift of God in Christ Jesus. Holiness is the evidence, not the wage. It is the letter of credibility of a living faith that understands the one who began a good work in us will be faithful to complete it when he brings us into his kingdom. And so section two summarizes the nature of the ship that was made for the ocean of good works. It was made to go into all the world and be a light reflecting the one who is himself light. It was made to bear the marks of saving faith by declaring in the ocean of life, we are his workmanship. Any questions so far? All right. Moving now to section three and their ability. A ship may know the course that the sovereign king has commanded and still lie helpless with no wind. And so we may ask from where does the power come to sail in the works that God has prepared beforehand? The power is not found in the ship. That's why I said a sailing ship. but wholly from the Spirit of Christ. Our confession states, their ability to do good works is not at all of themselves but wholly from the Spirit of Christ and that they may be enabled thereunto. Beside the graces they have already received, there is required an actual influence of the same Holy Spirit to work in them to will and to do of his good pleasure. Yet are they not hereunto to grow negligent, as if they were not bound to perform any duty unless upon a special movement of the Spirit, but they ought to be diligent in stirring up the grace of God that is in them. Two errors are refuted here in this section of the Confession. The first is the Pelagian self-sufficiency. Pelagius objected to Augustine's famous statement, O Lord, grant what you command and command what you will. Pelagius believed that God would not command us to do something that we could not in our own sufficiency accomplish. But the Lord Jesus Christ corrects this very error when he says, Apart from me, you can do nothing. apart from Christ we are a ship dead in the water the spirit of Christ the one who was over the face of the waters in Genesis 1-2 is the same one who breathes life into the sails of our fragile vessel the second error refuted here is lazy spiritualism that waits in the harbor for an extraordinary gust of wind to bring it out into the ocean and while it is true that the wind is from heaven the sails of the ship must still be loosened. This is an example of both God's sovereignty and man's responsibility. We are not to grow negligent as if we were not bound to perform the duty unless upon a special motion of the Spirit but we ought to be diligent in stirring up the grace of God in us. Ezekiel 36 speaks of their ability in the new covenant. It says, Then I will sprinkle clean water on you and you shall be clean. I will cleanse you from all your filthiness and from all your idols. I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you. I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes and you will keep my judgments and do them. God does not merely advise the stone to become flesh. He does not advise the ship to loosen its sail. He gives the heart and causes the ship to raise its sail The same God who saves us apart from our working causes the ship to sail in good works that he prepared beforehand 2 Corinthians 3 4 excuse me 3 verses 4 through 5 rightfully keeps the ship from boasting in itself when it says, and we have such trust through Christ toward God, not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think of anything as being from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God. And so even the thought of a sufficiency is not from ourselves. Every league of faithful sailing is a testimony to another's sufficiency. For it is he who said, my grace is sufficient for you. My strength is made perfect in weakness. 2 Corinthians 12.9. Philippians 2 likewise declares, therefore my beloved, as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you both to will and to do for his good pleasure. We must not wait to feel a special motion before we obey. God has commanded all people to keep his commandments, regardless of their ability. Therefore we obey because God has commanded us to obey, and we rejoice that he is already at work in the willing and the doing for his good pleasure. 2 Timothy 1, 6 and 7 forbids negligence and spiritual laziness when it says, Therefore I remind you to stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of hands. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind. And so stir up the gift. Raise the sail, or lower the sail, whichever term you use. Do not sit idly in the harbor and call negligence humility or spirituality. The ship that will not tend to its sail while waiting for a miracle has misunderstood the ordinary means of grace. jude 20 and 21 shows the ordinary means by which that stirring up takes place it says but you beloved building yourselves up upon your most holy faith praying in the holy spirit keep yourselves in the love of god looking for the mercy of our lord jesus christ unto eternal life building praying keeping looking these are the working out of our salvation with fear and trembling. These are not works of merit. They are the fruits and evidence of a saving faith looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. And so section three summarizes that sailing in good works is only possible because the Spirit of Christ works in us for his good pleasure. The ability to obediently sail the ocean of life is all of grace. the duty is all of obedience to what God has commanded in his word by being diligent in stirring up that grace of God that is in us. Moving now to our fourth and fifth section, and the limits of good works. The confession here seeks to protect the gospel from another error. Some would imagine that their sailing has merited wages from the sovereign Lord. but the scriptural truth is that even the highest obedience in this life is still only our duty. The confession states, they who in their obedience attain to the greatest height which is possible in this life are so far from being able to supererogate and to do much more than God requires as that they fall short of much which in duty they are bound to do. we cannot by our best works merit pardon of sin or eternal life at the hand of God by reason of the great disproportion that is between them and the glory to come and the infinite distance that is between us and God whom by them we can neither profit nor satisfy for the debt of our former sins but when we have done all we can we have but done our duty and are unprofitable servants and because as they are good, they proceed from his spirit and as they are wrought by us, they are defiled and mixed with so much weakness and imperfection that they cannot endure the severity of God's judgment. I know that's a long paragraph, but there are no wages owed to the claimless creature of the dust. The works that we walk in are good because they proceed from the spirit of God. They cannot justify because, as it says, wrought by us, they are stained. We'd say they are as stained as filthy rags. Justification remains not in us or from us, but fully in and from the imputed righteousness of Christ. Luke 17.10 declares, So likewise you, when you have done all those things which you are commanded, say, we are unprofitable servants. We have done what was our duty to do. I was thinking of some of the most faithful men and women of the church as I was preparing this lesson. And yet after the most fruitful life is lived in obedience, it is only our duty. And honestly, we all fail to even do that. Job 9, 2-4 answers the man who would contend with God on the basis of his record. It says, Truly I know it is so. But how can a man be righteous before God? If one wished to contend with him, he could not answer him one time out of a thousand. God is wise in heart and mighty in strength. For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God. For what does the scripture say? Abraham believed God and it was accounted to him for righteousness. Now to him who works, the wages are not counted as grace, but as debt. But to him who does not work, but believes on him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness. just as David also describes the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works. If our good works justified, then God's grace would become wages owed to us. But rather, God justifies the ungodly and imputes Christ's righteousness apart from our works. Boasting in ourselves is silence, just as Ephesians 2.9 requires. Isaiah 64.6 strips the last varnish from the deck of our tiny ship at any thought of self-righteousness. But we are all like an unclean thing, and all our righteousness are like filthy rags. We all fade as a leaf, and our iniquities like the wind have taken us away. And so even our best deeds are as filthy rags when brought before the holy and perfect God. The confession here refuses to let our good works stand in the place of Christ's obedience and his imputed righteousness. Titus 3, 4-7 But when the kindness and the love of God our Savior toward men appeared, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, that, having been justified by his grace, we should become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. So not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his mercy.
